newsitem.title: FRANCE: CADES outlines 1997 aims, plans MTN issues.
newsitem.headline: CADES outlines 1997 aims, plans MTN issues.

text.p: French welfare debt repayment fund CADES said on Tuesday it would continue to restructure its debt in 1997, borrowing prinipally in French francs but also in foreign currencies, notably dollars.

Benoit Jolivet, chairman of the fund, told a news briefing that borrowing would be mainly medium and long-term debt to lengthen the fund's duration. CADES was also authorised to proceed with a medium-term note (MTN) programme in francs and foreign currencies, and private placements, he said.
"We will continue to reduce our outstanding short-term debt and will continue to issue medium and long-term debt," Jolivet said. He added "the French franc market will remain our principal market."

The Caisse d'Amortissement de la Dette Sociale fund was launched in April 1996 to repay 140 billion francs of accumulated social security debt by January 2009, taking the burden off the welfare system.

He said CADES would cut its syndicated loan facility, which it is not using at the moment, to 30 billion francs from 60 billion, to save costs. However, the fund would continue to roll over its short term debt, issuing between 15 and 20 billion francs in 1997.

Jolivet said the duration of the fund, calculated before the issue of a $1 billion March 2002 bond due to be sold today, was 3.5 years. He said the average cost of the CADES funds, excluding commissions, was 5.6 percent.
Christophe Frankel, in charge of CADES market operations said, "The optimal duration should be higher, but not much."
Regarding the current maturities of bonds CADES has issued, Jolivet pointed out that there were two gaps in its maturity range at 2003 and 2006 which could be filled this year.

Jolivet said CADES would continue to try and create large liquid issues in francs, with a minimum outstanding of 10 billion francs, but its borrowing in other currencies would be more opportunistic and that issues would be around $1 billion.
"We will certainly continue to do operations in dollars," Jolivet said.

Within Europe, Jolivet said CADES was looking mainly at marks or guilders. He said the fund was not planning to issue any so-called "parallel bonds", bonds with the same characteristics but denominated in different currencies likely to take part in a single European currency.
He said the bonds were both complex legally and CADES was as yet unfamiliar with the investor base interested in such bonds. The fund would continue to do more "classic operations".
Frankel said CADES would consider floating rate bonds, such as bonds based on the French TEC 10 index, but that the market conditions for such bonds were "not so good" at the moment.
Jolivet said CADES would continue to look at yen issues, but that any decision would clearly depend on being able to swap the proceeds back into francs at good rate.
"I don't know if we will or we won't, but it's possible," Jolivet said.
He also said it was probable that CADES would pay less for its 2002 $1 billion dollar issue than borrowing in francs after the proceeds had been swapped back into francs.
